nameStory: The name 'camas' comes from the Chinook word 'chamas,' referring to the sweet, edible bulbs that were a crucial food source for Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. 'Great camas' distinguishes this larger species from its smaller relatives, with impressive flower spikes that can tower over other wildflowers.
description: Great camas is a striking perennial wildflower that grows from a deep bulb, sending up tall spikes of star-shaped blue to purple flowers. The plant typically reaches 2-4 feet tall, with long, narrow leaves that emerge from the base like a fountain of green ribbons. Though native to western North America, this eye-catching bulb occasionally appears in New England gardens and naturalized settings, where its dramatic flower spikes make it impossible to miss in late spring.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, tall spikes of 6-petaled star-shaped flowers ranging from deep blue to purple, each about an inch across with prominent yellow stamens that stick out noticeably

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves that arch gracefully from the base, feeling smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, with parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in a distinctive fountain-like clump with leaves radiating from the center and a single tall flower spike rising prominently above the foliage

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Three-chambered capsules that split open to reveal small, black, angular seeds that rattle when the dried pods are shaken

habitat: In New England, great camas is extremely rare in the wild, with only one documented observation, likely an escaped garden plant or deliberate planting. When cultivated, it thrives in moist, well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade, often planted in perennial borders or naturalized meadow settings.

seasonality.spring: Narrow leaves emerge early, followed by spectacular flower spikes in late spring that bloom for several weeks, attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, seed capsules develop while leaves remain green and photosynthetic, storing energy in the underground bulb.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, while seed capsules turn brown and split open to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Plant goes completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, surviving as a deep bulb until spring emergence.

funFact: The bulbs of great camas were so important to Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples that they managed entire meadows like farms, conducting controlled burns to prevent trees from taking over and maintain ideal growing conditions for this 'Indian potato.'
confusionNotes: The tall flower spikes might be confused with lupines, but camas has 6-petaled star-shaped flowers rather than lupine's pea-like blooms, and the leaves are much narrower and grass-like rather than palmately divided.
contextualKnowledge: While great camas bulbs are edible and nutritious, they can be easily confused with the deadly poisonous death camas (Zigadenus species) that often grows nearby in the wild, leading to the saying among Indigenous peoples: 'When in doubt, don't.'
compareHints: Great camas is much larger and more robust than its eastern relative Atlantic camas, with taller flower spikes and broader leaves. Atlantic camas is also extremely rare in New England, but when present, it has smaller, more delicate flowers and a more compact growth habit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Atlantic camas is the only Camassia species native to eastern North America, while great camas is a western species sometimes grown in gardens.
